lede.text: Hyderabad bangle makers roll lac over a brass or steel base, toymakers lacquer turned wood by rubbing lac sticks into it, pichhwai painters used red lac, and Nagercoil temple jewellery sets kemp stones in lac.

Jackfruit wood is usually preferred for Tanjore painting panels and makes the mridangam and the Thanjavur veena, while tamarind goes into the chalk primer of patachitra cloth, the coating of Cheriyal khadi and the paste that joins the veena's carved parts.

Sankhari craftsmen cut bangles from conch shell and Cheriyal painters took white from crushed sea shells, while gold foil grips kundan stones, gold leaf follows the gems embedded in Tanjore paintings, and a Jaipur miniature workshop beats gold foil thinner.

A miniature workshop's pigments included orpiment and cinnabar, rogan is usually coloured with trisulphide of arsenic and red lead oxide, toymakers use orpiment, and the glass refining mix is mostly arsenic trioxide.

sentences.text: Warli painters coat a smoothed mud wall with cow dung and geru, Gond walls and floors are covered in a white clay called chhui, and Sohrai comb-cutting draws patterns through wet white clay laid over black clay.
Meenakari is enamel painting used mainly in fine jewellery, its enamel made by crushing glass, and kundan sets gems with gold foil between the stones, a setting called jadau.
Sankhari craftsmen cut several bangles from a single conch of the sea snail Turbinella pyrum, while NABARD describes Sambhal's horn craft as fed by horns that local slaughterhouses discard.
Lac, secreted by lac insects, is the only natural resin of animal origin, and a model project profile names paraffin wax as the main raw material of candles.
Traditional wooden-toy making is conducted mainly at cottage-industry scale, most artisans operating independently, and Kathputli is a form of string puppetry practised in Rajasthan.

Indian musical instruments have been classified since ancient times into four heads, and the sustained tone of the mridanga and tabla comes from a heavy wooden shell and a drum-head loaded with an adherent composition.

India's bangles are almost exclusively produced in the Firozabad glass cluster, whose units mostly use silica sand with soda ash as flux, and Varanasi bead makers wind torch-melted glass onto a mandrel.
Chhau masks of clay and wood are used for chhau performances in West Bengal, Jharkhand and Odisha, and mask GIs also include the Majuli Mask of Assam and the Chamoli Wooden Ramman Mask.
Indian toys date back 5000 years to the excavated toys of Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro, and archaeologists found ample evidence of conch shell craft at Harappan sites.

Lac was known from at least the first millennium BCE, its name coming from the Sanskrit laksha, meaning 100,000, and until synthetic aniline dyes arrived in the late nineteenth century lac dye was the primary product of lac cultivation.

Raman noted that the mridanga is pictured in the Ajanta cave paintings, and the Thanjavur Veena's GI statement of case traces the instrument's history to the Sangam period, about 2,000 years ago, when its earlier form was called the yazh.

Ganjifa has been popular in the subcontinent since the sixteenth century, meenakari, originally a Persian art form, was brought to India in the sixteenth century, and kundan found great patronage among the Mughals.

Tanjore painting emerged in the early seventeenth century under Nayaka patronage, Cheriyal scroll painting has been practised since the seventeenth century, and historical references suggest Kathputli has been practised since the seventeenth century.

Hornell found the wearing of chank bangles confined in his day to Bengal and adjacent provinces, with Dacca the chief centre, and concluded that southern artisans settled in Dhaka during the fourteenth century or probably earlier.

In the second half of the nineteenth century factory-made pigments replaced plant and mineral colours in courtly painting across the subcontinent, and by the late nineteenth century Mysore painting had added synthetic vermilion, ultramarine, emerald green and crimson.
Firozabad's glass making dates from the Mughal period, and Arikamedu in Puducherry saw glass bead making where a Roman and Tamil trade relation is observed, its beads dating back to Roman times.
Sohrai painters take black from manganese-rich clay, red from red ochre and white from kaolin, while Gond painters make red from geru soil and yellow from an ochre clay called ramraj.
Mysore painters prepared their ground with powdered white lead and gum arabic, and Cheriyal painters took white from crushed sea shells, blue from indigo, black from soot and yellow from turmeric.

Kundan frameworks are commonly 22-karat gold with 24-karat gold foil hammered into the sides of the stones as a grip, and gold can hold most meenakari enamel colours while silver holds only pink, green and blue.

Raw conch shells come from the sea snail Turbinella pyrum of the Gulf of Mannar, and NABARD describes Sambhal's horns being divided into hollow and solid sections, then cleaned and sun-dried until they shed their smell.
Lac resin can be processed into shellac, shaped into jewellery or used to finish wooden surfaces, and lac-turnery uses three grades of lac, from light golden button lac to a dark black lac.
Hyderabad lac bangles are built on a brass or steel base, and paraffin wax, the main raw material for candles, is a controlled item that the state Directorate of Industries allocates.

A mridangam is made from a jackfruit trunk with parchments of goat, cow and buffalo skin, and sources differ on the veena: the NIOS textbook gives it a bowl of bottle gourd, while the Thanjavur veena is made of jackfruit wood.
Toymakers favour wood that is soft to moderately hard and easy to carve, and besides wood they use mogali leaves, ochre, orpiment, chalk powder, gums and pastes, and gurjan oil.
Analysis of forty-two pigments from a Jaipur miniature painter's workshop identified khariya as kaolinite, hinglu as cinnabar (HgS) and harital as orpiment (As2S3).
Pithora pigments are mixed with milk and mahudo, which functions as a binder, while Sohrai artists dilute their soil pigments with water and use no binders.

Rogan paste is castor-seed oil boiled for over twelve hours and thrown into cold water, usually coloured with trisulphide of arsenic, red lead oxide, white lead and indigo, though Impart found synthetic dyes increasingly used in 2022.
Meenakari enamel is made by crushing glass and mixing it with a liquid of pomegranate seeds and water, and lac dye takes its red from laccaic acid in the lac insect's body fluid.

In glass, silica is the former, soda ash the flux and limestone a stabiliser making soda lime glass insoluble in water, and the refining mix is mostly arsenic trioxide with nitrates of soda and potash.
In melting, soda ash forms low-melting alkali silicates with sand, which react with the high-melting constituents while the carbonates give off carbon dioxide.

Metallic oxides of iron, cobalt, copper and manganese colour the glass, selenium and cobalt oxide mask the greenish tint of iron, and phosphorus oxide or fluorine makes the opal glass Firozabad calls block or china glass.
Varanasi bead makers use emery powder (aluminium oxide), sulphuric acid and nitric acid to polish and wash their beads.

Raman showed that the mridanga and tabla, accompanying drums with loaded drum-heads, solve in practical form the problem of turning a circular drum-head's inharmonic overtones into a harmonic instrument.
In his 1919 results the loaded and damped drum-head suppressed all overtones above the ninth and grouped those nine into five tones in harmonic sequence.
The heavy wooden shell and the symmetrical loading of the drum-head sustain the tone, while the marginal leather ring acts as a damper on overtones.
A study of mridangam woods found jackfruit most favourable for its high SRC and similar impedance in different directions, its low density also lightening the drum.

Thin threads let tambura strings vibrate without touching the metal bridge, called jeeva or javaari in the north, and wind instruments sound through a vibrating air column, some through vibrating reeds as in the nagaswaram and shehnai.
Hyderabad lac bangle makers heat stones so that their hot base melts the lac surface and sticks as it cools, and Varanasi wooden-toy makers slowly heat each cut piece to draw out its moisture.
The Kathputli boli, a thin rubber tape stretched between two bamboo sticks and held between the puppeteer's lips, produces the whistle-like sound of a puppet's speech.
Firozabad bangle makers melt sand, ash and lime in a furnace at temperatures around 1350 °C.
In the Jaipur miniature workshop studied, pigments were prepared by ghutai, grinding them and mixing them with gum Arabic, and gold foil was beaten thinner by kutai.
Pithora walls are first coated with white clay and the border is drawn first, while Tanjore painters embed gems in spots of ground limestone and glue before applying gold leaf.
Kundan making runs from ghadayi through khudayi and meenakari to jadai, and meenakari enamel is fused to the base metal by heating and finished by boiling with a mild acid.
Hyderabad bangle makers heat lac on a wooden rod over a coal burner, press and roll it on an iron plate, and rub heated coloured lac over it.

For a turned toy the wood is cut, seasoned, turned on a manual or motor lathe and lacquered with lac sticks, while Varanasi's carved toys are dipped in distemper, painted with duco white and given a final coat of lacquer.

Firozabad glass bangle makers wind a glass thread into a spiral on a rotating iron mandrel, the belan, cut it lengthwise into loops and join each bangle's ends over a candle or kerosene lamp, a step called judai.

Varanasi bead makers use lamp winding, winding torch-melted glass onto a mandrel, and Seraikela and Purulia chhau masks are built by layering clay on a cane or wood base and covering the mould with papier mache.
In the model candle process, wick is wound in the moulds, and wax is melted, coloured and poured into them to cool before the candles are taken out.
Rogan, developed with linseed oil in Peshawar and Lahore, was made in Kutch with castor oil, easier to cultivate in its arid climate.
Kerria lacca is the most important cultivated lac insect, and a 2022 review reports that kusum, palas, ber and Ficus trees account for about 90% of India's lac production.
Kusmi and rangeeni are two strains of Kerria lacca, kusum being the major host for kusmi lac and palas for rangeeni lac.
The toymakers of Nirmal and Kondapalli depend on Givotia rottleriformis and those of Ettikoppaka on Wrightia tinctoria, while Kathputli makers prefer soft, light aardu wood to mango wood.
After the 2004 tsunami disturbed the temperature, salinity and sea floor the conch molluscs need, Turbinella pyrum harvests declined and raw conch costs rose.
Givotia rottleriformis is becoming scarce through overexploitation and forest degradation, and Ettikoppaka's artisans urgently need to shift to plantation species because Wrightia is becoming scarce.
The authors of a 2013 Unasylva article see an urgent need to conserve existing forests and to encourage alternative plantation-grown species for wooden toys.
Lac culture acts like an insurance crop in drought years and is a livelihood for tribal farmers in forests and sub-hilly tracts.
Painting GIs include Madhubani, Thanjavur, Mysore Traditional, Kangra, Cheriyal and Nirmal Paintings, the Sohrai-Khovar, Gond, Basohli and Banaras Mural paintings, and the Painting of Lanjia Saura.

Meenakari is done green and blue on silver in Lucknow, as pink gulabi mina in Varanasi and in gold mainly in Delhi, Jaipur remains a kundan centre, and Nagercoil, in Kanyakumari district, makes temple jewellery.

Rameswaram, Tuticorin and Tirunelveli in Tamil Nadu supply the bulk of raw conches, and the Sambhal horn and bone crafts, Kerala's brass broidered coconut shell crafts and Bankura Conch Shell are registered GIs.
In a 2022 review Jharkhand produced 54.6% of India's lac, ahead of Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal, and Hyderabad Lac Bangles and Lac of Purulia are registered GIs.

The jack wood for the veenai and for drums such as the mridangam comes from groves near Panruti in Cuddalore district, and the NIOS textbook names Tanjore, Trivandrum, Manamadurai, Chennai and Bangalore as instrument-making centres.

Uttar Pradesh holds GIs for the Amroha Dholak, Banaras Tabla, Pilibhit Bansuri and Banaras Shehnai, Assam for six Bodo instruments and the Assam Bihu Dhol, and Tamil Nadu for the Thanjavur Veenai and Narasinghapettai Nagaswaram.
Firozabad's glass units buy sand from Rajasthan or Uttar Pradesh and soda ash from Gujarat, and Firozabad Glass and Varanasi Glass beads are GIs of Uttar Pradesh.

Sources differ on Nirmal's state, a 2013 article placing its toymakers in Andhra Pradesh while the GI register lists Nirmal Toys and Craft under Telangana, and toy GIs also include Channapatna Toys & Dolls, Kondapalli Bommallu and Etikoppaka Toys.

In 2022 Impart reported rogan practised in India by only two families in Nirona and three in Viramgam, Wadhwan and Ahmedabad, and Impart wrote in 2022 that kundan's commercialisation had reduced its craftsmanship.
A 2022 review describes India as the world leader in lac production and export, producing more than 20,000 tons per annum.

An FAO case study found many old markets for Channapatna lacquerware collapsing with cheap plastic substitutes for children's toys, and a 2013 article says plastic 'made in China' toys once threatened Channapatna's toy industry.
Export traders often bypass women toymakers, which may be partly because women mostly use hand lathes and exporters prefer articles made on power lathes, which men are more likely to use.

A 2013 Unasylva article put Channapatna's wooden-toy craftsmen at more than five thousand, and a 2001 study found 50-60 families in Nirmal making their living from toys of Givotia rottleriformis wood.
In 2023 a Thanjavur veenai maker estimated 10 full-time veenai makers and many more part-timers there, together making about 30 veenais a month.

In 2011-12 India's market for glass products such as lighting, bangles and beads was about 1500 tonnes per day, and Firozabad melted its glass mostly with coal in 1995, while a 2012 manual found piped natural gas its major energy.

In the seventeenth century Tavernier noted a trade in cutting bracelets and charms that employed more than 2,000 persons in Dacca and Patna, which Hornell took to mean Pabna, and a leading Bag Bazar producer said a 2001 ban and the 2004 tsunami hit the conch trade.
Warli painting depicts humans, animals and plants with lines, triangles, squares and circles, and lihane, the Warli word for painting, also means writing.
Mysore painting uses low-relief gesso with selective gilding, whereas Tanjore painting used high relief and abundant gold-work.
A Mughal ganjifa pack has ninety-six typically circular cards in eight suits of twelve, and its variants include the ten-suited dashavatara ganjifa, Mysore chad, sawantwadi and ganjapa of Odisha.

Cheriyal scrolls reached up to twenty metres with as many as fifty panels, and pieces of kundan jewellery carry meenakari work on their reverse side, though kundan jadau crafted in 22-karat gold does not.
A conch's value depends on its white colour, a symbol of purity, and craftsmen now also make rings, brooches and pendants, while conch bangles with gold filigree fetch a higher price.
Hyderabad lac bangles are embellished with pearls, semi-precious stones, mirrors and beads, and Purulia chhau masks cover the whole face under wire halos decorated with beads and sequins.
Traditional toys depict history, mythology, folklore and plant and animal life, and traditional Kathputli puppets are 1.5 to 2 feet tall and worked with one to three strings.
Impart wrote in 2022 that Kathputli puppets used today are often taller and have legs, and Raman described the tabla as a modern variant of the mridanga made of two drums.
Babulal Marotia is aware that his pigments may harm his health and says he washes his hands thoroughly after every painting session.
Arsenolite and other mineral arsenicals have been used in Ayurvedic medicinal preparations, which may explain why arsenolite was available as a household material.

In 1995 Firozabad's finishing and decoration units, mostly employing women, worked in air highly polluted with dust and kerosene vapour, and outdated technology was seriously affecting workers' health.
